summary: Patricia Hernandez argues that Twitch's troubles in 2023 are not a decline from a golden era but the natural result of an unsustainable system tying live-service games, costly AAA development and streamer labor together. Using Turner "Tfue" Tenney's 2022 retirement and Imane "Pokimane" Anys's pivot away from all-day gaming as examples, it shows how Fortnite's weekly-update model pushed publishers toward live-service, crunch, and huge marketing spend. Streamers must constantly play new content to hold viewers, while games need streamers to stay visible and keep player counts healthy, producing burnout on both sides.
one_line: Polygon argues Twitch's burnout and industry strain stem from an unsustainable live-service system, illustrated by Tfue's retirement and Pokimane's pivot away from all-day streaming.
key_facts: Turner "Tfue" Tenney became famous after a kill against Tyler "Ninja" Blevins in 2019, and he retired from streaming in 2022.
Epic Games laid off 830 employees a few years after the Fortnite wave that raised billions of dollars for the publisher.
Twitch has over 30 million daily viewers, and it launched in 2011.
Fortnite set a standard of free weekly content updates, which Epic could afford because most of its profits then came from licensing its engine.
According to the note, 22% of purchased games on Steam are unplayed outright.
A mere two-day pause from streaming might mean a Twitch streamer losing thousands of paying subscribers.
The CMA's report on Activision Blizzard says a AAA game's development budget can range from $80 million to $380 million, and seasonal updates require $50 million to $65 million.
A 2018 report noted marketing budgets for some titles can equal 75% to 100% of development spending.
Tyler "Ninja" Blevins reportedly commanded a $1 million payday for streaming Apex Legends.
All 10 of the most-watched games on Twitch in 2022 were live-service games with regular updates.
Epic Games developers reported months of crunch with 70-to-100-hour weeks as Fortnite took off, and Diablo 4's developers also said they underwent crunch.
Imane "Pokimane" Anys announced in late 2022 that she would stop streaming all day and pivot to lifestyle and beauty content on short-form platforms like TikTok.

An anonymous AAA developer who was a former Twitch streamer said live-service games need roughly 20,000 players to avoid bad matchmaking and connections, and he is still recovering from streaming burnout.
Tenney said FaZe Clan, now a penny stock, tried to rip him off.
